While FIFO avoids this by always serving the oldest, it can cause delays if the queue becomes long and processes are slow. FIFO scheduling is a first-in-first-out algorithm that processes jobs based on their arrival order. It ensures that the oldest job in the queue is executed immediately, guaranteeing fair treatment for all arriving processes regardless of their relative timing. This simple rule creates a predictable and stable system where the earliest entry is always served first.

The core operation involves maintaining a queue where the head of the line holds the most recent job. When a process arrives, it is added to the front of this queue, and the oldest job is removed and executed next. This structure prevents any process from waiting indefinitely for a slot, ensuring that the system remains efficient and responsive.

A practical example involves a server managing multiple online applications. If Application A arrives first, it is processed before Application B, which arrives later. This order ensures that the most active or earliest-requested service is handled promptly, preventing any single process from monopolizing resources.

The primary advantage of FIFO is its simplicity and fairness. It treats all processes equally by prioritizing those that have entered the system first, avoiding the inefficiencies of other policies like round-robin or priority-based scheduling. This makes it ideal for systems with limited resources where fairness is paramount.

Head-of-line blocking occurs when a process waiting in the queue cannot proceed until the oldest job is completed. This can cause delays for processes that arrive late, as they must wait for the queue to clear. However, this limitation is often acceptable in real-world scenarios where system stability is more important than minimizing waiting time for all processes.

Compared to other policies, FIFO is generally less efficient than round-robin or priority-based methods because it ignores the relative speeds of different processes. While it is simple, it may result in longer average wait times for processes that arrive later. Nevertheless, its simplicity and fairness make it a robust choice for many distributed systems and real-time applications.
